claims.claim: World history studies large-scale patterns, connections, and exchanges across many societies rather than telling the story of one nation, using comparison across societies and analysis of the connections between them as its two central moves.

World historians commonly organize the human past into a rough, contestable sequence of eras — deep prehistory, the first cities and states, a classical era, a post-classical era, an early modern era, and a modern era — while recognizing that these boundaries are conventions that fit some regions better than others.

The AP World History: Modern framework organizes the course around six themes — Humans and the Environment (ENV), Cultural Developments and Interactions (CDI), Governance (GOV), Economic Systems (ECN), Social Interactions and Organization (SIO), and Technology and Innovation (TEC) — and spans c. 1200 CE to the present.

Recurring world-history themes include human-environment interaction, the development and interaction of cultures, states and governance and conflict, economic systems and trade/exchange networks, and the movement of people and ideas.

Complex, literate societies with cities and states developed independently in several separate regions — including Mesopotamia, the Nile Valley, the Indus Valley, northern China, Mesoamerica, and the Andes — so no single region can be treated as the origin from which civilization spread to the rest of the world.

Conventional world histories have carried a Eurocentric bias, visible even in map projections that render Europe larger and the Global South smaller than their actual size, and in whose sources survive and get read.

UNESCO launched the General History of Africa in 1964; it now comprises 11 volumes written with a two-thirds-African International Scientific Committee, and it was created to overcome hegemonic, colonial, and Eurocentric perspectives and to reaffirm Africa's central place in humanity's shared history.

At the world scale, historians still distinguish established facts (what happened and when) from interpretation (why it happened and what it meant), and world-scale narratives remain open to revision as evidence and perspectives change.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How to divide world history into periods, and whether labels like 'classical' and 'medieval/post-classical' are appropriate outside Eurasia.
positions: A shared six-part periodization (prehistory, early civilizations, classical, post-classical, early modern, modern) makes global comparison tractable.
Such schemes were built from European and Mediterranean experience and distort regions, such as the Americas and sub-Saharan Africa, whose chronologies do not align with them.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Present the common scheme explicitly as a rough, contestable convention rather than a natural fact, and note that dates and labels are debated and region-dependent. The lesson uses 'c.' and 'roughly' for all era boundaries.
